newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T sees smoke, not fire in Liggett settlement.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T sees smoke, not fire in Liggett settlement.

text.p: British tobacco and insurance group B.A.T Industries Plc said on Friday a rival's decision to settle U.S. tobacco litigation would not force it to seek a similar pact, even though U.S. legal fees cost it tens of millions of pounds a year.

Liggett Group became the first tobacco company on Thursday to admit smoking was addictive and could cause cancer when it settled with 22 U.S. attorneys general who had sued to recover health care costs for smokers.
"We will not go out seeking a settlement," said B.A.T spokesman Ralph Edmondson. "Any move (like Liggett's) will not be initiated by the tobacco companies."

Liggett broke ranks with an industry which has successfully defended a plethora of court cases spanning five decades, by agreeing to pay 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next quarter of a century to 22 U.S. states.
The states' legal claims are only a fraction of the hundreds of other U.S. lawsuits filed against tobacco companies over the past few years but are considered to be potentially the most damaging.
The 22 states are seeking to prove U.S. tobacco companies consistently lied about the dangers of cigarettes.

"I believe this is the beginning of the end for this conspiracy of lies and deception that has been perpetrated on the American public by the tobacco companies. Somebody is finally telling the truth," Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods told a news conference on Thursday.

Liggett, the smallest of the U.S. tobacco companies with a two percent market share, has also agreed to allow current and former employees -- including its lawyers -- to testify against the rest of the industry.
B.A.T shares plunged six percent in early trade in London on Friday as investors worried Liggett would reveal a "smoking gun" which would prove the states' cases.
They later recovered to stand down six pence at 483 pence at midsession. But analysts doubted any significant new information would be forthcoming.
"This is all hype. I can't believe Liggett has documents which the other tobacco companies don't have," tobacco shares analyst Tom Bennett of investment bank Banque Paribas said.
He noted that under U.S. "discovery rules", U.S. tobacco companies have already provided a large quantity of documents to U.S. state legal authorities.

B.A.T said its U.S. division Brown & Williamson had already provided the states with around 12 million pages of documents. "If you lined them up end to end they would stretch from London to Warsaw," Edmondson said.

The legal settlement appeared to be a ploy by Liggett owner Bennett LeBow to get another tobacco company to acquire his group, he said. By settling legal liabilities, Liggett would become a more attractive takeover candidate to a larger company, analysts said.

Edmondson said that the $100 million B.A.T spent annually on legal fees was just part of the cost of doing business in the United States. The publicity surrounding the court cases had not hurt its business.

"Even after those costs Brown & Williamson is making $1 billion a year pre-tax," Edmondson said. "Over the past two years there has been virtually no downward movement in cigarette consumption in the U.S. despite all of this noise."

Tobacco shares have recovered in recent months amid indications the U.S. government might be moving towards a settlement of tobacco-related litigation. B.A.T itself said earlier this month that it would be sensible to evaluate a settlement, which chief executive Martin Broughton said should cover all current and future claims and as approved by Congress and the White House.
